aws-mastery-global-infrastructure.core: AWS's global infrastructure is a hierarchy of failure domains: partitions (hard legal boundaries), regions (geographic isolation), availability zones (independent data centres) and hundreds of edge locations, plus Local and Wavelength Zones for extreme latency needs. Architecture should match these boundaries.

first_principles.problem: Designs that ignore physical layout fail when a data centre or region has problems, or feel slow to distant users.
derivation: **Multi-region** for disaster recovery and global users.

analogy.title: A global logistics network
analogy.story: Countries, regional hubs, local depots and doorstep lockers, each with its own failure and delivery-time profile.
analogy.breaks: Logistics moves goods; AWS moves data, which can be replicated rather than shipped.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Every layer adds a failure domain to survive.

check.q: Which boundary protects against a single data-centre fire?
check.a: Availability zones: deploy across multiple AZs.

aws-mastery-iam-architecture.core: IAM decides every AWS request: authenticate the principal, start from implicit deny, let explicit denies win, require all guardrails (SCPs, boundaries, session policies) to permit, and require an allow from identity or resource policies. Cross-account roles and ABAC scale access safely.

first_principles.problem: Cloud security failures usually stem from over-broad or misunderstood permissions.

analogy.title: Layered building security
analogy.story: Country laws, building rules, floor restrictions and your personal badge all have to agree.
analogy.breaks: Buildings rarely change rules hourly; IAM policies change constantly and need automation.

example.title: Multi-account access model
flow: Humans sign in via Identity Center
SCPs restrict regions and protect logging
ABAC by team tag inside accounts

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Layers combine for least privilege at scale.

check.q: What does an SCP do?
check.a: Sets the maximum permissions for principals in member accounts; it never grants permissions.

aws-mastery-advanced-networking.core: AWS networking at scale replaces pairwise peering meshes with Transit Gateway hubs, exposes services privately through gateway and interface endpoints, makes traffic visible with flow logs, and accelerates global users with CloudFront and Global Accelerator.

first_principles.problem: Simple VPC designs break with many accounts, regions, on-prem links and security needs.
truths: Private service access reduces exposure and cost.
Visibility is required for debugging and security.

analogy.title: National transport infrastructure
analogy.story: Hub airports, private service roads, traffic cameras and express lanes.
analogy.breaks: Transport is physical; network paths are configured and can change instantly.

example.title: An enterprise network
flow: TGW per region, peered across regions

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Each tool solves one scaling problem.

check.q: Why is VPC peering unsuitable for 100 VPCs?
check.a: It's non-transitive and pairwise, needing thousands of connections and route entries.

aws-mastery-compute-internals-nitro.core: EC2 runs on the Nitro System, which offloads I/O to dedicated cards, roots trust in a security chip and uses a tiny hypervisor, giving near bare-metal performance. Choose instance families by CPU:memory needs, control physical placement with placement groups, and cut costs with diversified Spot capacity.

first_principles.problem: Compute choices made blindly waste money and performance.
truths: Spare capacity is cheap but interruptible.

analogy.title: Renting the right vehicle from a modern fleet
analogy.story: Well-maintained engines, the right body type, parking close together or apart, and cheap standby rentals.
analogy.breaks: Rentals take days to swap; instances take minutes.

check.q: What's the warning period before a Spot interruption?
check.a: Two minutes.

storage-deep-dive-s3.core: S3 is far more than a bucket: strongly consistent, extremely durable object storage with storage classes and lifecycle rules for cost, Object Lock for immutability, Athena for in-place queries and presigned URLs for secure direct access.

first_principles.problem: Using S3 naively wastes money and leaves data exposed or unprotected.
truths: Durability and immutability can be built in.

analogy.title: A smart warehouse
analogy.story: Auto-archiving, tamper-proof vaults, on-site analysts and temporary visitor passes.
analogy.breaks: Warehouses fill up; S3 has no practical capacity limit.

example.title: A logging data lake
flow: Logs land as Parquet partitioned by day
Lifecycle: IA at 30d, Deep Archive at 180d

check.q: Which S3 feature protects backups from deletion by compromised admins?
check.a: Object Lock in Compliance mode.

storage-deep-dive-ebs.core: EBS gives EC2 persistent, AZ-scoped block storage. Pick volume types by IOPS, throughput and latency (gp3 by default, io2 for critical databases), use Multi-Attach only with cluster-aware software, and protect data with incremental snapshots automated by DLM.

first_principles.problem: Wrong volume choices waste money or throttle databases, and unmanaged backups fail when needed.
truths: Block storage must be close to compute.

analogy.title: Drives in a server room
analogy.story: Choose fast or big drives, share them only with cluster software, and back them up nightly.
analogy.breaks: Physical drives are fixed; EBS can change type and size live.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Match type to role; automate protection.

check.q: Which EBS type is the sensible default?
check.a: gp3.

storage-deep-dive-efs-fsx.core: When many servers need a shared filesystem, AWS offers EFS (elastic NFS for Linux) and FSx: Windows File Server (SMB + AD), Lustre (parallel HPC/ML), NetApp ONTAP (multi-protocol enterprise features) and OpenZFS (low-latency NFS). Choose by protocol, performance and feature needs.

first_principles.problem: Block and object storage don't serve shared-file workloads well.

analogy.title: Choosing the right shared workspace
analogy.story: An expandable office, a Windows-only suite, a racetrack, a multi-tool workshop and a quick-turn studio.
analogy.breaks: Workspaces are leased for years; file systems can be created per job.

check.q: Which file service suits Windows apps with AD permissions?
check.a: FSx for Windows File Server.

database-engineering-aurora.core: Aurora rebuilds the relational database for the cloud: the log is the database, six-way quorum storage spans three AZs, endpoints abstract topology, Serverless v2 scales in seconds and Global Database replicates across regions in under a second. Choose it over RDS when you need its scale and availability.

first_principles.problem: Traditional databases on block storage struggle with replication lag, failover time and scaling.

analogy.title: A newsroom with a shared live ledger
analogy.story: Reporters write edits to a ledger copied in three buildings; editors anywhere read the same ledger.
analogy.breaks: Ledgers are read by humans; storage serves pages to instances in milliseconds.

example.title: An e-commerce database
flow: Serverless v2 replicas for sales spikes

check.q: How many storage copies does Aurora keep, and across how many AZs?
check.a: Six copies across three AZs.

database-engineering-dynamodb.core: DynamoDB delivers consistent single-digit-ms performance at any scale by designing tables around access patterns: partition and sort keys, single-table designs, overloaded GSIs, sharding for hot keys, capacity maths, Streams for side effects and conditional writes or transactions for correctness.

first_principles.problem: Relational habits applied to DynamoDB produce scans, throttling and inconsistency.

analogy.title: A high-speed postal sorting system
analogy.story: Every letter's address determines its bin instantly; you design the addresses around how letters will be collected.
analogy.breaks: Postal addresses are fixed; you can redesign keys, but migrations are costly.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Every pattern served by a key or index.

check.q: What's the first step in DynamoDB design?
check.a: Listing the application's access patterns.

serverless-event-driven-lambda.core: Lambda runs code in Firecracker microVMs that initialise once and serve many warm invocations. Manage cold starts with good init code, SnapStart or provisioned concurrency; control capacity with reserved concurrency; share dependencies with layers; and tune event source mappings for reliable batch processing.

first_principles.problem: Serverless apps suffer latency spikes, throttling and stuck event processing without understanding the runtime model.

analogy.title: A taxi rank with drivers on call
analogy.story: Some cars are warm and waiting, new ones take time to arrive, and dispatch manages the queue.
analogy.breaks: Taxis take one fare at a time, and so does each Lambda environment, but Lambda scales out far faster.

example.title: Order processing pipeline
flow: Worker Lambda via ESM, batch 10, partial failures

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Tune each knob to its role.

check.q: What's the difference between reserved and provisioned concurrency?
check.a: Reserved guarantees and caps how many concurrent executions a function can use; provisioned keeps environments pre-initialised to avoid cold starts.

serverless-event-driven-eventbridge.core: EventBridge is AWS's event router: producers publish JSON facts to buses, rules match patterns and deliver at least once to targets, schemas formalise contracts, Pipes handle point-to-point flows, and archive/replay plus DLQs make the system operable.

first_principles.problem: Tightly coupled service calls make systems fragile and hard to extend.
truths: Delivery is at least once and unordered.

analogy.title: A city's postal and courier network
analogy.story: Senders post letters; sorting centres route them to whoever subscribed.
analogy.breaks: Post goes to one address; events can fan out to many subscribers.

check.q: What delivery guarantee does EventBridge provide?
check.a: At-least-once delivery, without ordering guarantees.

serverless-event-driven-sqs-sns.core: SQS and SNS decouple services: SQS buffers work for one consumer group (standard for throughput, FIFO for order), SNS fans messages out to many subscribers, visibility timeouts and DLQs handle failure, and long polling keeps consumers efficient.

first_principles.problem: Synchronous coupling spreads overload and failures across services.
truths: Failures must be retried and isolated.

analogy.title: A postal system with sorting centres and PO boxes
analogy.story: Mail is broadcast to subscribers' boxes, collected at each person's pace, with undeliverable mail set aside.
analogy.breaks: Post doesn't reappear if not collected; SQS messages do after the visibility timeout.

example.title: Image processing platform
flow: Workers long-poll and autoscale on depth

check.q: Which SQS setting prevents two consumers processing the same message concurrently?
check.a: The visibility timeout.

management-governance-ssm-cfn-config.core: Governance at scale means treating infrastructure as cattle: define it in CloudFormation, operate it through Systems Manager without bastions, record every API call with CloudTrail and continuously evaluate configuration with AWS Config rules and remediation.

first_principles.problem: Manual operations and invisible changes make large environments insecure and unrepeatable.

analogy.title: A well-run factory
analogy.story: Machines built from specs, operated from a control room, with cameras and inspectors on the floor.
analogy.breaks: Factories change slowly; cloud environments change thousands of times a day.

example.title: Baseline for every new account
flow: Org trail already covers the account

check.q: Which tool replaces bastion hosts for shell access?
check.a: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager.

security-services-kms-guardduty-waf.core: AWS security services form layered defences: KMS encrypts data with keys that never leave HSMs (including multi-Region keys for DR), GuardDuty detects threats from logs, WAF and Shield block application and DDoS attacks, and Macie finds sensitive data in S3.

first_principles.problem: No single control can protect cloud workloads from every attack.
truths: Encryption limits impact of data theft.

analogy.title: A bank's security system
analogy.story: Vault encryption, alarms, guards at the door, flood defences and auditors checking where valuables are kept.
analogy.breaks: Banks have a few doors; cloud apps have thousands of APIs.

example.title: Securing a public API
flow: CloudFront + WAF managed rules + rate limits

check.q: Which service blocks SQL injection at the edge?
check.a: AWS WAF.

cost-management-cur-savings-plans.core: Taming the AWS bill means visibility (Cost Explorer for trends, CUR for detail), attribution (enforced tags, accounts per team, showback and chargeback), alerts (budgets, anomaly detection) and commitments (Savings Plans and RIs) sized to steady baseline usage.

first_principles.problem: Cloud spend grows unchecked when nobody sees or owns it.
truths: Baseline usage is cheaper with commitments.

analogy.title: Household budgeting
analogy.story: Track every expense, assign categories, set alerts for overspending and lock in cheaper annual contracts for regular bills.
analogy.breaks: Household bills are stable; cloud usage can triple overnight.

check.q: Why commit to baseline rather than peak usage?
check.a: Commitments are paid regardless of use; peak usage is temporary, so committing to it wastes money.

aws-well-architected-framework.core: The Well-Architected Framework guides design and review across six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability. Regular reviews surface risks and trade-offs, producing a prioritised improvement plan.

first_principles.problem: Architectures accumulate hidden risks across many concerns.
truths: Concerns trade off against each other.

analogy.title: A periodic health check-up
analogy.story: Heart, lungs, diet and habits are all checked, and a plan follows.
analogy.breaks: Bodies age predictably; architectures change with every deploy.

example.title: Annual review cycle
flow: WA Tool review per critical workload

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Reviews are a habit, not an event.

check.q: Which pillar was added most recently?
check.a: Sustainability.

control-plane-vs-data-plane.core: Control planes change resources; data planes do the work. Data planes are more available, so reliable designs never put control planes in the request path, recover through pre-provisioned, statically stable capacity and data-plane failover (Route 53 health checks, ARC), avoid fragile red buttons and contain failures with cells.

first_principles.problem: Recovery plans and request paths that depend on APIs fail exactly during big outages.

analogy.title: Keeping a ship sailing when the radio dies
analogy.story: Engines (data plane) keep running, compartments contain leaks, and lifeboats are already lowered.
analogy.breaks: Ships face one storm; services face many overlapping failures.

example.title: Hardening a payments API
flow: ARC routing controls for region failover

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Resilience is designed before the outage.

check.q: What is static stability?
check.a: A system's ability to keep working through a failure without needing to make changes or call control-plane APIs.

advanced-dynamodb-modeling.core: Advanced DynamoDB modelling treats data as a graph served by keys: adjacency lists with inverted GSIs for many-to-many, write sharding for hot keys, sparse indexes for filtered work lists, and an access-pattern matrix to combine them coherently.

first_principles.problem: Complex relationships and skewed traffic break naive DynamoDB designs.

analogy.title: An expertly organised warehouse
analogy.story: Cross-referenced shelves, extra loading bays for bestsellers and a clipboard of urgent orders.
analogy.breaks: Warehouses can be reorganised over a weekend; table redesigns need careful migrations.

check.q: Why document an access-pattern matrix?
check.a: It ensures every query is served by a key or index and guides safe evolution of the model.

karpenter-vs-cluster-autoscaler.core: Node autoscaling resolves Pending pods. Cluster Autoscaler scales pre-defined ASG node groups; Karpenter provisions best-fit EC2 instances directly from flexible NodePools, bin-packs tightly and consolidates, expires and replaces drifted nodes under disruption budgets.

first_principles.problem: Slow or rigid scaling causes outages during spikes and waste during lulls.

analogy.title: Fleet management for a delivery company
analogy.story: Hire the right van for each load, combine half-empty routes and retire old vans on schedule.
analogy.breaks: Vans are leased for years; nodes can live minutes.

example.title: A cost-optimised EKS cluster
flow: Karpenter NodePool: Spot + On-Demand, c/m/r, arm64+amd64

check.q: What's Karpenter's main advantage over Cluster Autoscaler?
check.a: It provisions best-fit instances directly without node groups, scaling faster and packing more efficiently.

networking-physics-dx-gwlb-efa.core: When standard networking falls short, Direct Connect provides private physical links with BGP for hybrid connectivity, Gateway Load Balancer inserts scalable third-party appliances transparently using GENEVE, and EFA gives HPC and ML workloads OS-bypass, low-latency networking.

first_principles.problem: Hybrid, security-inspection and HPC workloads need network properties that VPNs and ENIs can't deliver.

analogy.title: Specialised transport infrastructure
analogy.story: Dedicated freight lines, customs lanes and express tubes for specific needs.
analogy.breaks: Transport infrastructure is permanent; these services are provisioned in minutes to weeks.

check.q: Which service keeps source IPs intact while inserting firewalls inline?
check.a: Gateway Load Balancer.

isolation-zones-cells-stability.core: Bounding blast radius layers isolation: regions and AZs for physical failures, static stability so nothing must change to survive, cells as complete bulkheads for software and tenant failures, shuffle sharding to make full overlap between tenants unlikely, and progressive deployment through all layers.

first_principles.problem: Shared infrastructure turns individual failures into total outages.

analogy.title: Ship design
analogy.story: Hull compartments, lifeboats ready, separate engines and careful sea trials.
analogy.breaks: Ships face known seas; software faces novel failure modes.

check.q: Name three blast-radius techniques.
check.a: Cell-based architecture, shuffle sharding and static stability (also AZ/region isolation and progressive deploys).

containers-orchestration-eks.core: EKS gives you upstream Kubernetes with an AWS-run, multi-AZ control plane. You choose the data plane (managed nodes, Karpenter, Fargate), plan pod IPs with the VPC CNI and prefix delegation, keep core components current as managed add-ons and give each workload least-privilege AWS access via IRSA or Pod Identity.

first_principles.problem: Running Kubernetes on AWS well requires bridging Kubernetes abstractions with AWS networking and identity.
truths: Control planes are hard to run.

analogy.title: A franchise in a managed mall
analogy.story: The mall handles structure and security; you design the shop, staff badges and stock rooms.
analogy.breaks: Malls rarely force upgrades; Kubernetes versions expire on a schedule.

check.q: Which EKS feature gives each pod its own IAM role?
check.a: IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) or EKS Pod Identity.

containers-orchestration-ecs.core: ECS is AWS's native, free-control-plane container orchestrator: task definitions describe containers and IAM roles, services keep fleets healthy and deploy safely, and capacity providers connect tasks to Fargate, Fargate Spot or EC2. It trades Kubernetes' ecosystem for simplicity.

first_principles.problem: Teams need reliable container orchestration without excessive operational overhead.
truths: Fleets need reconciliation and safe deploys.

analogy.title: A franchise operations manual
analogy.story: Standard recipes, a manager keeping staff levels right and agencies supplying workers.
analogy.breaks: Franchises change slowly; services redeploy many times a day.

example.title: A production ECS service
flow: Task def with secrets + task role
Service behind ALB, circuit breaker on

check.q: What keeps a desired number of ECS tasks running?
check.a: An ECS service.

containers-orchestration-fargate.core: Fargate runs containers in per-task microVMs without hosts to manage, billed per second for requested resources. Platform 1.4.0 routes all traffic through the task's own ENI, so plan IPs and endpoints, and cut costs with right-sizing, ARM, Spot and Savings Plans.

first_principles.problem: Managing container hosts is toil that small teams can't afford.
truths: Pricing trades unit cost for zero idle.

analogy.title: Using taxis for all company travel
analogy.story: No fleet to maintain; you plan pick-up points and pick cheaper ride options.
analogy.breaks: Taxis are always available; Fargate Spot can be interrupted.

example.title: Migrating from EC2-backed ECS
flow: Add VPC endpoints for private pulls

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Serverless still needs network and cost planning.

check.q: What Fargate purchase option suits interruptible batch jobs?
check.a: Fargate Spot.

compute-scaling-asg.core: Auto Scaling groups keep EC2 fleets healthy and elastic: launch templates define instances, scaling policies follow demand, lifecycle hooks make launches and terminations graceful, warm pools cut boot time, and instance refresh rolls out changes safely.

first_principles.problem: Static fleets waste money or fail under load, and changes to them are risky.

analogy.title: A smart taxi depot
analogy.story: Standard cars, more on the road at rush hour, pre-warmed standbys and careful rotation for servicing.
analogy.breaks: Taxis take a while to recruit; instances can be added in minutes, or seconds with warm pools.

example.title: Web tier for a sale event
flow: Predictive scaling from last year's pattern

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Combine features for both speed and safety.

check.q: Which ASG feature reduces scale-out time for slow-booting apps?
check.a: Warm pools.

api-gateway-edge-networking.core: API Gateway is the managed front door for APIs: choose HTTP or REST APIs by needed features, pick edge, regional or private endpoints, throttle with token buckets and usage plans, authorise with JWT or Lambda authorizers, and connect backends through proxy, direct service or private integrations.

first_principles.problem: APIs need consistent security, limits and routing without every service reimplementing them.

analogy.title: A building's front desk and switchboard
analogy.story: Security checks, visitor quotas and routing calls to the right office or service.
analogy.breaks: Front desks handle hundreds of visitors; API Gateway handles thousands per second.

example.title: Partner API platform
flow: API keys + usage plans per partner

check.q: Which API type is cheaper and faster for simple Lambda proxies?
check.a: HTTP APIs.

api-gateway-edge-networking-cloudfront-a.core: Advanced CloudFront engineering layers caching (edge, regional caches, Origin Shield), runs logic at the right edge tier (CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge), restricts content with signed URLs or cookies and origin access control, and engineers lean cache keys with per-path behaviours for high hit ratios.

first_principles.problem: A CDN configured with defaults leaves origins overloaded, content exposed and caches ineffective.
truths: Edge logic should be minimal and close.

analogy.title: A global distribution network for a publisher
analogy.story: Local shops, regional depots and one central warehouse, with membership cards and clear product labels.
analogy.breaks: Publishers ship physical copies; CDNs serve the same bytes to millions instantly.

check.q: What most affects CloudFront's cache hit ratio?
check.a: The cache key: which query strings, headers and cookies are included.

route-53-deep-dive.core: Route 53 is a global traffic controller built on DNS: hosted zones and alias records, routing policies (weighted, latency, geolocation, geoproximity, failover, multivalue) for shaping traffic, and distributed health checks that make answers change automatically during failures.

first_principles.problem: Static DNS can't steer users to the best or healthiest endpoint.
truths: Answers can depend on policy and health.
TTLs bound how fast changes apply.

analogy.title: An air traffic controller for user requests
analogy.story: Routes each flight to the best runway and diverts when one closes.
analogy.breaks: Controllers talk to each plane; DNS answers are cached by resolvers.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Policies nest to meet several goals.

check.q: Which routing policy supports gradual canary releases?
check.a: Weighted routing.

caching-search-elasticache.core: ElastiCache (Valkey/Redis OSS, Memcached) serves data from memory in sub-milliseconds. Choose Redis/Valkey for features and HA, cluster mode for horizontal scale, Global Datastore for multi-region, and manage memory with eviction policies, jittered TTLs and careful invalidation to avoid staleness and stampedes.

first_principles.problem: Databases can't serve every repeated read at scale and low latency.
truths: Hot keys and expiries cause spikes.

analogy.title: A busy bar's speed rail
analogy.story: The most-ordered bottles within arm's reach, restocked from the cellar, with old bottles rotated out.
analogy.breaks: Bottles don't change contents; cached data may silently diverge from the database.

example.title: E-commerce caching layer
flow: Cache-aside for products with 5-min jittered TTL

check.q: Which Redis feature distributes keys across shards?
check.a: Cluster mode enabled with hash slots.

memorydb.core: MemoryDB is a durable, Redis/Valkey-compatible in-memory database: writes commit to a Multi-AZ transaction log before acknowledgement, clusters shard and replicate across AZs, snapshots cover operator errors and DR, and failover promotes caught-up replicas without losing acknowledged writes. Use it when Redis data is the source of truth.

first_principles.problem: Redis is fast but traditionally not durable enough as a primary store.

analogy.title: A high-speed bank teller with an instant ledger
analogy.story: Fast service, but every transaction is recorded before the receipt prints.
analogy.breaks: Bank ledgers are audited daily; MemoryDB's log is continuous and automatic.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: One fast, durable store instead of cache + DB.

check.q: When should you choose MemoryDB over ElastiCache?
check.a: When Redis-format data is the primary source of truth and must be durable.

opensearch-advanced-architecture.core: Production OpenSearch separates cluster management (dedicated masters) from data work, tiers storage from hot to UltraWarm (S3 + cache) to cold with ISM policies, and federates across clusters with cross-cluster search for queries and cross-cluster replication for regional copies and DR.

first_principles.problem: Search and log clusters become unstable and expensive at scale.
truths: Management must be insulated from data load.

analogy.title: A national library system
analogy.story: A coordinating office, busy branches, deep archives, a federated catalogue and replicated collections.
analogy.breaks: Libraries change slowly; log clusters ingest terabytes daily.

example.title: Global logging platform
flow: ISM: 7 d hot → 30 d warm → 1 y cold
Product search uses CCR to EU

check.q: Which feature lets one cluster query indices on other clusters?
check.a: Cross-cluster search.

streaming-messaging-kinesis.core: Kinesis Data Streams provides ordered, replayable shards for custom real-time processing, with enhanced fan-out for many consumers. Firehose delivers streams into storage with buffering, format conversion and partitioning. Choose Kinesis for event streams with multiple readers, and SQS for task queues.

first_principles.problem: Real-time data needs ordered, scalable ingestion and delivery to many consumers and stores.

analogy.title: A broadcasting network with recording studios
analogy.story: Live channels, many receivers and an archive service writing everything to tape.
analogy.breaks: TV is one-to-many passively; stream consumers must checkpoint progress.

example.title: Real-time analytics pipeline
flow: Firehose → S3 Parquet partitioned by date

check.q: What determines which shard a record goes to?
check.a: The hash of its partition key.

amazon-msk-kafka.core: Amazon MSK delivers Kafka's APIs and ecosystem without infrastructure toil: brokers across AZs with durable replication, KRaft to remove ZooKeeper, tiered storage for cheap long retention and a Serverless option that removes capacity planning for variable workloads.

first_principles.problem: Kafka is valuable but painful to operate at scale.

analogy.title: Leasing a fully serviced logistics hub
analogy.story: Your goods and routes, their buildings, staff and maintenance.
analogy.breaks: Logistics hubs don't rebalance themselves; Kafka partitions still need thoughtful design.

check.q: What does tiered storage reduce in MSK?
check.a: The cost of long retention, by moving older segments off broker disks to a cheaper remote tier.

identity-auth-cognito-user-pools.core: Cognito user pools are a managed user directory and OIDC provider: OAuth code flow with PKCE issues verifiable JWTs, managed login handles UI and federation, key settings (identifiers, MFA, clients) must be chosen carefully, and Lambda triggers customise sign-up, sign-in, tokens and migration.

first_principles.problem: Building secure authentication from scratch is slow and error-prone.

analogy.title: A managed passport office for your app
analogy.story: It verifies identities, issues documents and lets you add local procedures.
analogy.breaks: Passports last years; tokens should expire in minutes to hours.

example.title: SaaS login stack
flow: Pre token trigger adds tenant_id claim
API Gateway JWT authorizer checks scopes

check.q: What does a user pool's refresh token do?
check.a: Obtains new ID and access tokens without the user signing in again.

identity-auth-cognito-identity-pools.core: Cognito identity pools vend temporary AWS credentials in exchange for identities (user pool, social, SAML, guest), mapping users to IAM roles, so apps can call AWS services directly. Policy variables give per-user data isolation, and user pools remain the choice for authenticating to your own APIs.

first_principles.problem: Client apps need direct AWS access without embedded keys or over-broad permissions.

analogy.title: A hotel key-card system
analogy.story: Reception verifies you, the card opens only your room, and it expires at checkout.
analogy.breaks: Hotel cards are physical; credentials can be copied, so keep them short-lived.

check.q: What prevents users from reading each other's S3 files with a shared role?
check.a: IAM policy variables restricting resources to the caller's own identity ID prefix.

cloudwatch-advanced-insights-filters-ala.core: Advanced CloudWatch replaces grepping servers with centralised logs, Logs Insights queries, metric filters (and EMF) that turn logs into alertable metrics, and composite alarms that combine signals into precise, low-noise pages.

first_principles.problem: Distributed, ephemeral systems make logs hard to find and alerts noisy.
truths: Metrics are cheap to alarm on.

analogy.title: A modern control room
analogy.story: All feeds centralised, searchable footage, counters for key events and smart alarms.
analogy.breaks: Control rooms watch live; logs also need retention and cost planning.

example.title: Checkout observability
flow: JSON logs with order_id, status, latency
EMF metrics for latency and failures
Saved Insights queries in the runbook

check.q: What turns a log pattern into a CloudWatch metric?
check.a: A metric filter (or emitting EMF-formatted logs).

deep-observability-xray.core: Distributed tracing with X-Ray follows each request across services: SDKs send segments over UDP to a local collector, sampling rules control cost, segments and subsegments reveal where time goes, annotations make traces searchable, and the service map shows live architecture health.

first_principles.problem: In microservices, latency and errors hide among many hops.

analogy.title: Parcel tracking for requests
analogy.story: Every depot scans, you can search by customer, and a live map shows where delays build.
analogy.breaks: Parcels are tracked 100%; traces are sampled.

check.q: What's the difference between a segment and a subsegment?
check.a: A segment records a service's work for a request; subsegments record calls and code blocks within it.

backup-recovery-aws-backup.core: AWS Backup turns scattered scripts into policy: tag-based plans with tiered schedules and lifecycle, cross-region and cross-account copies to escape blast radius, and Vault Lock to make backups immutable against compromised admins, all with audit reports and regular restore tests.

first_principles.problem: Inconsistent, deletable backups fail exactly when you need them.
truths: Backups share blast radius unless isolated.

analogy.title: A bank's records protection
analogy.story: Automatic archiving, copies in another city's vault, time locks and regular audits.
analogy.breaks: Bank records are paper; restores must be tested to prove they work.

example.title: Ransomware-resilient backup
flow: Org backup policy on all accounts
Copies to central backup account (separate KMS)

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Backups you can't delete and know you can restore.

check.q: Which feature prevents even root from deleting recovery points?
check.a: Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode.

cli-sdk-setup.core: The CLI and SDKs automate AWS through the same APIs as the console. Set them up safely with SSO-based profiles, understand the credential provider chain, handle MFA requirements properly, and write SDK code with explicit sessions, retries and pagination.

first_principles.problem: Manual console work is error-prone, and misconfigured credentials cause leaks or wrong-account actions.
truths: Credentials resolve in a fixed order.

analogy.title: A professional's toolbox, properly labelled and maintained
analogy.story: The right key for each site, safety checks before use and tools that don't slip.
analogy.breaks: Toolboxes sit in a van; credentials live on disk and can be stolen.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Safety and correctness from the start.

check.q: What's the first credential source checked after explicit parameters?
check.a: Environment variables.

hybrid-cloud-edge-outposts-ssm.core: Hybrid and edge architectures exist because of physics (latency, bandwidth) and law (residency). AWS extends its model outward with Outposts (AWS racks on site), Local Zones, Snow and Greengrass, and manages any server through SSM hybrid activations, so one set of APIs and tools spans everywhere.

first_principles.problem: Workloads that must stay local otherwise create a separate, inconsistent operating model.
truths: Some data and compute must stay local.
Each hybrid tool fits a constraint.

analogy.title: Franchise branches following head-office systems
analogy.story: Local premises, shared processes and tools.
analogy.breaks: Branches can run offline indefinitely; some AWS edge options need regional connectivity.

check.q: Which service lets you manage on-prem servers with Session Manager and Patch Manager?
check.a: AWS Systems Manager via hybrid activations.

aws-iot.core: AWS IoT connects physical devices securely and at scale: IoT Core is the authenticated MQTT broker, device shadows keep desired and reported state for intermittently connected devices, Greengrass runs logic at the edge offline, and the Rules Engine routes messages into AWS services.

first_principles.problem: Fleets of constrained, intermittently connected devices need secure messaging, control and data pipelines.
truths: Each device needs its own identity.

analogy.title: A postal and command system for machines
analogy.story: ID cards, mailboxes, notes on the fridge, local managers and sorting machines.
analogy.breaks: People read mail when convenient; devices may be offline for days.

example.title: Smart building platform
flow: Sensors with certs publish via MQTT

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Each piece handles a device reality.

check.q: Which IoT feature lets apps set device state while it's offline?
check.a: Device shadows (desired state).

euc-workspaces-appstream.core: End-user computing on AWS streams work environments while data stays central: WorkSpaces for persistent (or pooled) desktops, AppStream 2.0 for ephemeral application streaming, and persona-based VDI patterns that balance experience, security and cost.

first_principles.problem: Distributing sensitive work to unmanaged devices is risky and slow.
truths: Pixels can travel instead of data.

analogy.title: A secure office accessed through a window
analogy.story: You see and work with everything, but nothing leaves the building.
analogy.breaks: Windows are free; streaming needs bandwidth and low latency.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Data never leaves; access is easy.

check.q: What core security benefit does cloud VDI provide?
check.a: Data stays in AWS; endpoints only receive streamed pixels.

control-tower-landing-zones.core: Control Tower builds and governs a multi-account landing zone: Organizations with policy-driven OUs, Log Archive and Audit accounts, Identity Center access, Account Factory vending (and AFT for GitOps), and layered controls: preventive SCPs, detective Config rules and proactive CloudFormation hooks.

first_principles.problem: Many accounts without central governance become insecure and unmanageable.

analogy.title: A managed estate of apartment buildings
analogy.story: Central security, records, standard flats on demand and building codes enforced throughout.
analogy.breaks: Estates grow slowly; organisations can add hundreds of accounts a year.

example.title: Scaling to 200 accounts
flow: OUs: Security, Infra, Prod, NonProd, Sandbox

check.q: Name the three types of Control Tower controls.
check.a: Preventive, detective and proactive.

aws-vpc-lattice.core: VPC Lattice replaces network wiring with a service directory: services and target groups register into service networks, consumer VPCs associate, requests are proxied at layer 7 (so overlapping CIDRs are fine), and IAM auth policies enforce zero-trust per request. Use it alongside Transit Gateway and PrivateLink where each fits.

first_principles.problem: Service-to-service connectivity across many VPCs and accounts becomes a routing and security maze.

analogy.title: A corporate directory with door badges
analogy.story: Look up the service by name, and your badge decides whether you get in.
analogy.breaks: Directories don't carry calls; Lattice proxies the traffic too.

example.title: Microservices across 30 accounts
flow: One service network shared via RAM
TGW kept for data and hybrid

check.q: What authenticates requests in Lattice with AWS_IAM auth type?
check.a: SigV4-signed requests evaluated against IAM auth policies.

nitro-enclaves.core: Nitro Enclaves protect highly sensitive processing from even root users on the host: an isolated VM carved from the instance's CPUs and memory, with no disk, network or console, talking only via vsock, and proving its exact code to KMS through hardware-signed attestation.

first_principles.problem: Privileged users and malware on an instance can read secrets in memory.
truths: Trust needs proof of code identity.

analogy.title: A sealed vault inside a bank with a verified courier slot
analogy.story: Only verified documents pass through, and no staff can enter.
analogy.breaks: Vaults can be opened in emergencies; enclaves can't be accessed interactively.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Shrink who and what you must trust.

check.q: What lets KMS verify it's talking to a specific enclave image?
check.a: The attestation document's PCR measurements, checked against key policy conditions.

aws-fis-chaos-engineering.core: AWS FIS brings chaos engineering in-house: experiments with actions, scoped targets and alarm-based stop conditions, OS-level faults through SSM documents, and a game-day workflow that starts small, communicates clearly and turns findings into fixes and automated tests.

first_principles.problem: Resilience designs are assumed to work until a real failure proves otherwise.

analogy.title: A flight simulator for your architecture
analogy.story: Practise engine failures safely so pilots and planes handle the real thing.
analogy.breaks: Simulators are virtual; FIS faults affect real resources.

check.q: What three things does every FIS experiment template need?
check.a: Actions, targets and stop conditions (plus an IAM role).
